# Optimize the capability — ship several REAL, SAFE, VERIFIED prompt fixes this iteration

## THE READER (who consumes what you edit)
At runtime these capabilities are read by `rits/google/gemma-4-31B-it` — capability tier: **strong**. The reader is a capable general model, but less robust than frontier on long or ambiguous context. Keep instructions clear and reasonably explicit; add a worked example for tricky formats; prefer code enforcement for behavioral rules over trusting inference.
Optimize your edits for THIS reader's capability level, not for your own. When the reader is weaker than you, prefer explicit rules, worked examples, and code enforcement over terse prose you would personally infer.


Focus: every failing task on the val split. Current val reward 0.725: 29 solid / 0 flaky / 11 failing of 40 tasks.



GOAL: raise the eval score as much as you can THIS iteration, then STOP (the harness
re-scores you — don't run evaluation yourself). The capability under optimization is
PROSE: the agent's prompt / skill text. There are no tool implementations to edit here.

Make **AS MANY real fixes as you can this iteration — solve many issues across many
trajectories, not just the biggest one.** A timid one- or two-edit iteration is an
under-used iteration: diagnose EVERY failure cluster in `./trajectories/` and ship a fix
for each one that passes the three tests below. Breadth is the goal — the more distinct
failing clusters you fix in this ONE candidate, the larger the gain.

The ONLY brake on breadth is regression: every edit must pass all three tests, because a
single speculative edit that breaks a passing task can sink an iteration of good work (it
did in prior runs). So the discipline is "many fixes, each one real and safe" — NOT "few
fixes". Do not stop at the first cluster; work through them all.

## WHAT YOU MAY EDIT — and the two ways iterations get wasted here
Edit ONLY the capability files listed in `## What you are editing (the allowed edit space)
The capability under optimization is composed of these editable artifact(s). Use the FULL edit space below — do not limit yourself to trivial wording tweaks.
- **system-prompt** — Optimize an agent's system prompt / policy text (instructions, output contract, decision policy).
  - Allowed edits: Edit the prompt/policy text: instructions, decision policy, and the output contract. Prefer sharpening rules the traces show the agent breaking; do not just append more preamble.
  - Full guidance (read it): ./guidance/system-prompt/SKILL.md` below (the prompt / skill text in
this working directory). Everything else you can see is READ-ONLY CONTEXT.

**You may NOT edit the adapter, the harness, the scorer, the benchmark, or the
environment** — not to make a task pass, not to fix a broken mount or a missing binary,
not "just to unblock the run". Those files are how your score is MEASURED; changing them
does not improve the capability, and a gain obtained that way is not a result. An
iteration that edits infrastructure has produced NOTHING measurable, however green the
number looks. **If the traces show an ENVIRONMENT fault** (permission denied, missing
binary, gateway/network error, timeout, container failure — the same error on nearly every
task, unrelated to the task's content), then the correct and complete action is:
1. do NOT edit the prompt to work around it (a prose workaround for a broken environment
   is a speculative edit that fails the REAL test — the prompt is not the defect), and
2. state the diagnosis in `PROCESS.md` and `JOURNAL.md` precisely — the exact error, how
   many tasks it hit, and what a human must fix — then STOP. Handing back an accurate
   "the environment is broken, here is the evidence" is a SUCCESSFUL iteration.

**The other way iterations get wasted: another prose rule for a behavior the agent already
knows.** When the agent has the rule and skips it anyway, adding a second sentence saying
the same thing changes nothing — you must change the STRUCTURE that makes it skippable
(see the levers below): make the step unavoidable and ordered, make the contract explicit,
or give a worked example it can pattern-match. Prose is for genuine KNOWLEDGE gaps (a
fact / format / criterion the agent cannot derive) and for STRUCTURE that changes what the
agent does — not for repetition or emphasis.

## The THREE TESTS every change must pass (this is the whole game)
Before you keep any edit, confirm all three. Drop any edit that fails even one.
1. **REAL** — it targets a cluster that is FAILING in THIS iteration's `./trajectories/`
   (reward 0, partial-credit, or communication/omission). Never edit for a hypothetical
   problem, and never edit on account of a task whose failure is an environment fault.
2. **SAFE (bounded blast radius)** — the real regression question is *behavioral*:
   **would this edit change what the agent DOES on ANY currently-passing task?** Two
   blast-radius classes:
   - **BOUNDED** — an ADDITIVE rule that applies only under a stated condition present in
     the failing cases, or a clarification of an output contract the passing tasks already
     satisfy. This is the SAFE default — prefer it.
   - **UNBOUNDED** — any edit to a GLOBAL decision/permission/refusal rule, or a rewrite /
     reordering / deletion that changes the instruction the agent follows on every task. It
     changes behavior across the ENTIRE class, including tasks where the original behavior
     was the gold answer. Allowed ONLY if the new behavior is correct for EVERY task in
     that class AND you have read the currently-passing tasks in the class and confirmed
     none relied on the old wording.
   Name the passing tasks in each edit's blast-radius class and state which class it is.
   A regression wastes the whole candidate (the gate rejects a net-zero), not one task.
3. **VERIFIED** — you have shown it actually fixes its target (see VERIFY-THE-FIX). An
   edit you cannot verify is a guess — drop it.

Quality AND breadth: ship every fix that passes the three tests — the more clusters you
cover safely, the bigger the gain. The only edits to leave out are the speculative ones
(an edit that fails a test), not real fixes you ran out of patience for. Don't re-add
anything `LEDGER.md` / `JOURNAL.md` show was already tried and rejected.

  missing-rule, worked example, ordered procedure, consolidation of conflicting text). Do
  not invent change types from memory — take them from the skill, and deliberately apply
  MULTIPLE DIFFERENT types this iteration, matching each cluster to the strongest type the

- `./guidance/diagnose/SKILL.md` — the failure-clustering method. Use it.

- `./LEDGER.md` — FACTS (read-only): every prior iteration's outcome + the exact tasks it
  broke/fixed. Your SAFE test starts here — never re-introduce a change that broke a task.
- `./JOURNAL.md` — the accumulating handover. Each entry is the optimizer's INTENT, and

  what worked: read them all before proposing. If the most recent RESULT is **REJECTED**,
  its batch was reverted; read that entry's `./prior_iterations/<id>/diff.patch`, keep the
  edits that did NOT appear in its `broke={...}`, and DROP or REDESIGN the ones that did —
  do NOT resubmit the whole rejected batch, and do NOT abandon the cluster. APPEND your new
  entry (intent only) below the marker; never edit earlier entries or re-try a refuted idea.
- `./RUNMAP.md` + `./prior_iterations/<id>/` — EVERY prior iteration's (accepted AND

- `./guidance/optimizer/<name>.md` — your agent's subagent/parallelism features (optional).


## Process (do this, then STOP)
**Parallelism:** Your agent supports parallel subagents/worktrees (see ./guidance/optimizer/claude-code.md). FAN OUT to cover MANY clusters at once: one read-only subagent per trajectory-group to diagnose, then one edit-subagent per issue (each in its own worktree), then MERGE every edit into this ONE candidate with no conflicts. This is how a single iteration fixes many issues across many trajectories, not just the biggest one.
1. Read your capability SKILL(s) + the diagnose method + the cross-iteration files
   (LEDGER facts, JOURNAL handover, RUNMAP for clusters you'll touch).
2. Diagnose THIS iteration's `./trajectories/` ONLY (not stale signatures). Cluster ALL
   failures by shared root cause — total, partial-credit, AND communication/omission.
   **First separate ENVIRONMENT faults from capability failures** (see above): a cluster
   whose every trace dies on the same infrastructure error is not yours to fix.
   RANK the remaining clusters by LEVERAGE = (# failing tasks × trials × score
   recoverable), biggest first — but plan to fix ALL of them this iteration.
3. For EACH cluster, pick the strongest improvement TYPE from the capability SKILL(s)
   (cross-check the FAILURE TYPE section next) and draft the edit. Across the iteration
   use MULTIPLE different types from the skills, not the same one repeatedly. Run each
   edit through the THREE TESTS; keep it only if it passes all three.
4. Ship every passing edit together in this ONE candidate — cover as many clusters as you
   can SAFELY (that is the win), and never include an edit that fails a test.
5. Fill `PROCESS.md` and APPEND your entry to `JOURNAL.md`. STOP.

## Choose the lever by FAILURE TYPE
Pick the strongest lever your capability's edit space offers (see `./guidance/<cap>/`).
Every lever below is a PROSE edit — the point is that they are not all the same edit.

- **OUTPUT-CONTRACT / FORMAT MISS** — the work is right but the graded artifact is wrong
  (written to the wrong place, wrong shape, wrong precision, formula instead of value,
  extra cells/keys touched). **Default strong lever: state the contract exactly, once, in
  imperative form, at the point of use** — the precise path/shape/type, what must NOT be
  touched, and the one-line check the agent can run before finishing. This is the
  highest-yield, lowest-regression prompt edit; reach for it first.
- **SKIPPED / OUT-OF-ORDER STEP (behavioral)** — the agent knows the rule and skips it, or
  acts before verifying. Do NOT restate the rule. **Make it structurally unavoidable:** an
  ORDERED, numbered procedure with the step as a precondition of the next one, or a
  short pre-finish checklist the agent must satisfy — phrased as work to perform, not as
  advice to remember.
- **CAPABILITY GAP / ACTION STALL** — the agent has no reliable way to do the thing, or it
  narrates a multi-step action then never executes it. Prose CANNOT invent a missing
  capability: what it can do is supply the concrete METHOD — a worked, copyable procedure
  (the exact sequence, API/idiom, and end-to-end example) that the agent can execute
  directly. If no wording could make the task achievable, say so in PROCESS.md rather than
  shipping a hopeful paragraph; a hard zero does not move on emphasis.
- **KNOWLEDGE GAP** — a format/criterion/fact the agent genuinely cannot derive → state it
  precisely, and only it. Don't restate a rule the agent already has; that's a skipped
  step (use structure), not a knowledge gap.
- **DECISION / PERMISSION (ACT vs REFUSE)** — the agent made the wrong call on a decision
  the prompt governs. **This is the most dangerous cluster to fix wrong.** NEVER loosen,
  broaden, or alter a GLOBAL decision/permission/refusal rule — a global change (e.g.
  "restricted records MAY now be modified") flips behavior for the WHOLE class and
  regresses every currently-passing task where the stricter behavior was the gold answer
  (this exact mistake sank a prior run). Instead add an ADDITIVE rule that NARROWS: state
  the exact discriminating CONDITION that separates the qualifying cases, so only those
  change.
- **CONFLICT / BLOAT** — two instructions disagree, or the rule that matters is buried in
  prose the agent skims. CONSOLIDATE: resolve the contradiction and hoist the decisive
  rule to where it is read. Deleting is allowed here — but only text you have shown to be
  redundant or contradicted, never a rule a passing task depends on.

Also fix **recovery guidance** — what the agent should do when its own attempt errors —
when a recoverable error stranded it mid-task. High leverage, low risk.

## VERIFY-THE-FIX (do this for EACH kept edit — it satisfies the VERIFIED + SAFE tests)
A prompt edit cannot be unit-tested, so verify it against the TRACES, concretely:
- **Point at the evidence:** quote the line(s) from the failing trace that the edit
  addresses, and state what the agent would have done differently had the edit been
  present. "It would have been clearer" is not verification.
- **Contract / format edit:** confirm the value you now state matches what the SCORER
  compares (read the answer/expected artifact in the trace or the benchmark source) — not
  merely what the old prompt said. A confidently-stated wrong contract is worse than none.
- **Structural edit (ordered procedure / checklist):** confirm the skipped step is now a
  precondition of a step the agent must take, not just mentioned earlier.
- **Decision / permission edit:** the SAFE check is BEHAVIORAL. Enumerate the
  currently-passing tasks in the SAME decision class and confirm the edit would NOT flip
  the agent's action on any of them — in particular that it does not make the agent newly
  ACT where a passing task's gold answer was to refuse. If you cannot enumerate and check
  that class, the edit is UNBOUNDED and unverified — rescope it to the qualifying cases.
- **Deletion / consolidation:** name the tasks whose traces show the removed text was
  unused or contradicted, and confirm no passing trace relies on it.

Record one line per edit in PROCESS.md, e.g.
`trace <task>: wrote formula not value → contract line "write literal values"; passing <ids> already write literals`.
An edit with no verification line is unverified — verify it or drop it.

## NON-OVERFITTING (every edit must GENERALIZE)
Every edit encodes a GENERAL rule that holds across the whole class of inputs — NEVER a
literal that special-cases one task (its id, target, name, or expected answer), and never
the answer itself. ALLOWED: constants the domain defines (a fixed threshold, a required
path shape, a domain enum). Use per-task specifics and any ground-truth in the traces ONLY
to understand the failure CLASS, then write the general fix.

## Handover (REQUIRED before you STOP)
- **PROCESS.md** (this iteration): the ranked cluster list (with leverage + CONTRACT/
  STRUCTURE/KNOWLEDGE/DECISION tag), every kept edit + its lever, the VERIFY-THE-FIX +
  blast-radius line per edit, any ENVIRONMENT fault you diagnosed and handed back, what you
  deliberately skipped and why, and (if you used subagents) that you did.
- **JOURNAL.md** (append ONE entry below the marker; never edit earlier entries). Write
  INTENT only — you cannot know your gate result; the framework stamps the RESULT below
  your entry: the changes I made (1 line/edit, naming the section + cluster) · the
  EXPECTED effect + why each is safe · which prior RESULTS I built on and which regressing
  edits I did NOT re-try (cite ids) · refuted hypotheses (a prior RESULT disproved — never
  re-test) · high-value clusters not yet cracked + designs already tried · plateau signal +
  which lever to switch to · focus next iteration.

## How your edit is judged
Algorithm: hill-climb:all. Your edited candidate is re-scored on the SAME held-out val tasks and compared to the current best (val reward 0.725). It is ACCEPTED only if the per-task improvement clears a significance bar (a noise margin), so a tiny or lucky change is rejected. Aim for a real, generalizing gain across a CLASS of failures — not a one-off patch to a single task (that overfits and gets rejected or hurts the held-out test).

## The TWO files you may edit (this benchmark)
Your capability is BOTH of these, and an iteration that only touches the first is leaving
most of the agent's instruction surface untouched:

1. **`prompt.md`** — the agent's SYSTEM message: who it is, how it should work, what to
   check. ~40% of the words the agent reads.

2. **`task_template.md`** — the agent's FIRST USER message: how the job is framed, what each
   field means, and the interaction contract. ~60% of the words the agent reads. It is
   ordinary prose and you may reword, restructure, add to, or DELETE from it — including
   guidance that is actively unhelpful. (Read it critically: a line telling the agent it is
   finished as soon as an output file exists will discourage it from verifying values, which
   is the most common way tasks fail here.)

   The `{placeholders}` in it are filled in per task and are LOAD-BEARING. Keep every one of
   `{instruction}` `{spreadsheet_path}` `{spreadsheet_content}` `{instruction_type}`
   `{answer_position}` `{output_path}`; `{max_turns}` is optional; invent no others; write a
   literal brace as `{{` or `}}`. Break that and EVERY task scores 0 — the agent is never
   told where to write its answer — so the candidate is rejected outright.

Decide per cluster which file is the right place to fix it, and say which you chose in
PROCESS.md.


## Run budget — THIS MAY BE YOUR LAST ITERATION (iteration 1/1 (0 after this one); 0/1 consecutive rejects)
Update `META_INSIGHTS.md` and `FRAMEWORK_IMPROVEMENTS.md` THIS iteration — there may be no next one to do it in.

## Cross-iteration files in THIS working dir (clean ownership — read all)
- `LEDGER.md` — FACTS (framework, read-only): every iteration's outcome + the tasks it MEASURABLY broke/fixed, plus the ones whose move was under 2·SE and so resolves nothing. Never re-introduce a change that broke a task; never redesign an edit because a task landed in `unresolved`.
- `JOURNAL.md` — HANDOVER (yours, append-only across the whole run): read the whole thing, then APPEND your entry for this iteration below the marker line. Do NOT edit earlier entries. This is how you avoid repeating refuted ideas and hitting the same plateau.
- `PROCESS.md` — EXPLAINABILITY (yours, REQUIRED this iteration): fill it in as you work (ranked issues, every edit + class, verify-the-fix, subagents/features used, what to preserve, what you skipped). It is snapshotted with your candidate.
- `RUNMAP.md` + `./prior_iterations/<id>/` — every prior iteration's PROCESS.md + capability diff, copied in for you. Read the ones targeting your cluster BEFORE proposing, so you build on prior work instead of repeating it.
- `INSIGHTS.md` — SUMMARIZED, VERIFIED findings (yours, append-only, optional most iterations): a distilled 'what worked / what didn't / what's promising' a future iteration reads INSTEAD of the whole journal. Add an entry whenever you have a new CONFIRMED finding (cite the RESULT that confirmed it).
- `META_INSIGHTS.md` — about the SEARCH PROCESS itself (yours, append-only): which strategies helped or stalled, what to try next. Update AT LEAST once, at the end of the run.
- `FRAMEWORK_IMPROVEMENTS.md` — cross-run suggestions for cap-evolve ITSELF, not this task (yours, append-only, optional): what confused you or was missing about the framework. Update AT LEAST once, at the end of the run.
- `.capevolve/run_suite/rejected.jsonl` — ALREADY-REFUTED approaches (framework, read-only; JSON lines, one per rejected candidate with the gate's reason). Read it and make each proposal STRUCTURALLY different from what is in it. Its sibling `history.jsonl` is the same record for accepts.

name: PROCESS.md
text:
# PROCESS — what I did this iteration (explainability; REQUIRED)

Iteration 1/1 (only iteration of the run). Parent = seed, val 0.725 (29 solid / 11 failing of 40).
**`prompt.md` was EMPTY (0 bytes) in the seed** — the agent ran with no system message at all,
and 100% of its instruction surface was `task_template.md`. That is the single biggest
untouched lever in this run, so this iteration authors `prompt.md` from scratch and
restructures the template's interaction contract.

No prior iterations exist (`RUNMAP.md` and `LEDGER.md` are empty; `rejected.jsonl` /
`history.jsonl` are absent). So there is nothing to build on and nothing refuted to avoid —
the whole SAFE burden falls on reading the 29 passing traces, which I did.

## Environment faults: NONE found
Every one of the 40 traces executed python successfully and produced an output file. No
permission errors, no missing binaries, no gateway/timeout failures, no container faults.
`rollout.error` is `None` on all 40. Every failure is a capability failure. (One environment
FACT, established below and load-bearing for the edits: no formula evaluator exists in the
sandbox — zero of 40 traces contain `data_only=True`, `soffice`, `libreoffice`, `pycel`,
`formulas`, `xlwings`, or `subprocess`.)

## Two facts I established BEFORE editing, because they invalidate the obvious fix

1. **The grader RECALCULATES formulas.** Passing tasks 42198, 52807, 41589, 39515, 49801 each
   wrote an Excel formula string with openpyxl, never computed a value, and scored **1.0**.
   11842 wrote 96 formulas and 94/96 recalculated to the expected value. So the tempting rule
   "write literal values, not formulas" would be FALSE and UNBOUNDED — it would have flipped
   5+ passing tasks. I narrowed it instead to the exact subclass that genuinely cannot
   survive openpyxl: **array/CSE formulas** (`MEDIAN(IF(...))` etc.), which openpyxl writes
   as scalar formulas so the inner condition collapses to the range's first cell.
2. **Cell-Level grading checks only `answer_position`.** So the "collateral damage from
   `pandas.to_excel`" argument is fatal only for Sheet-Level (341-40: 955 wrong cells, ALL
   of them cells it was never asked to touch, while its 8 requested cells were correct;
   535-20: 257 wrong, column selection correct). I therefore justified Rule 1 on fidelity
   and kept an explicit escape clause, rather than banning `to_excel` — 11 PASSING tasks use
   `to_excel` and must not be disturbed.

## Ranked issue list (clusters by # failing tasks, biggest first)

| rank | cluster | tasks | shared root cause | tag | planned change class |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Vacuous verification** — the "verify" turn cannot fail | 11/11 (all) | Template said "re-open output_path and print the values you wrote". Agents obeyed literally and printed something that must agree: formula text from a non-`data_only` handle (33722, 49036, 42354, 11842, 53647), hand-typed constants (38985), or a read-back using the SAME wrong offset as the write (48924, 5835). Zero information; agents then stopped confidently at 3–6 turns while scoring 0. | STRUCTURE + KNOWLEDGE | Ordered staged procedure + falsifiable pre-finish checklist (template); "Python is your only oracle" (prompt) |
| 2 | **Full-sheet `to_excel` destroys untouched cells** | 341-40, 535-20 (+ contributes to 5835, 51359, 38985) | `read_excel` → mutate → `to_excel` converts text-stored numbers/dates, blanks→empty, headers→`Unnamed: N`, drops trailing cols. Both Sheet-Level failures had CORRECT requested edits and failed 100% on collateral damage. | CONTRACT/KNOWLEDGE | State the in-place openpyxl idiom as the default, with an escape clause for generate/re-shape (prompt Rule 1) + Sheet-Level before/after diff (template stage 3.4) |
| 3 | **Array-formula written as scalar formula** | 33722, (mechanism behind 53647's error text) | openpyxl has no `ArrayFormula` wrapper here; `MEDIAN(IF(cond,range))` recalculates against the first cell only → "different value of the right type". | KNOWLEDGE | Narrow additive rule naming the exact formula subclass (prompt Rule 3) |
| 4 | **Coordinate/off-by-one via `df.iloc` offsets** | 48924 (fatal, whole answer shifted 1 row), 5835 (read window `iloc[2:19]` for `C3:C19`), 38985 | `read_excel(header=0)` makes `iloc[0]` == Excel row 2; a second `+1` shifts everything. Read-back reused the same arithmetic, so the bug was invisible. | STRUCTURE | "Address graded cells by literal A1, write and read back by the same address" (prompt Rule 2 + template stage 3.1) |
| 5 | **Evidence in the workbook read then discarded** | 38985, 48924, 49036, 42354, 11842 | Pre-filled worked-example rows and explicit bound cells were printed and then contradicted; 42354 overwrote 5 already-correct cells with formulas that resolved to `#N/A`. | KNOWLEDGE + STRUCTURE | Mandatory stage-1 inspection of `answer_position` (template) + "treat what's there as a spec" (prompt Rule 4) |
| 6 | **Format/scope literalism** — decimals, blanks, one-past-the-end | 49036 (`"0%"` vs required `.00` → `67%` not `66.67%`), 42354 (wrote `""` into a must-be-blank cell + 1 cell past the range) | Instruction stated the format; agent noticed the conflict in a comment and guessed. | KNOWLEDGE | Prompt Rule 5 |
| 7 | **Stated caveat asserted away instead of handled** | 11842 (94/96 — "each person has two rows" → 2 cells HIGHER), 38985 (duplicate lookup values), 51359 | Agent wrote a comment claiming its approach "will correctly" handle the warned-about trap, and never printed a number proving it. | STRUCTURE | Prompt Rule 5 bullet 2 ("show the number, don't assert") |
| 8 | **No-op re-runs / silent ambiguity resolution** | 51359 (3 write+verify rounds, byte-identical `4.0 6.0 9.0 4.0` each time, never noticed), 33722, 49036 | No recovery guidance for "my own fix changed nothing". | RECOVERY | Prompt Rule 6 + template closing line |

Also failing and covered: **53647** (in the failing traces but not in the instruction's list of
11 — formula → error text + `str` where `float`/`int` expected; covered by clusters 1/3).

## Changes made this iteration

| cluster | edit class (from system-prompt SKILL) | file | what & why it generalizes | protects passing? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| all | **#7 add role/goal line + #8 tighten output contract** — new "How you are scored" section | `prompt.md` (new file) | States what the grader actually compares: values in `answer_position`, **including python type**; blank-vs-value; error strings; and that Sheet-Level grades the whole region. This is a fact no trace shows the agent knowing, and it is the domain's fixed contract, not a task specific. | Yes — describes the grading the 29 passing tasks already satisfy |
| 2 | **#4 add a rule the source requires** + **#5 worked example** | `prompt.md` Rule 1 | Default = `load_workbook` → assign A1 cells → `save`, with a 5-line copyable idiom; explicit escape clause for "generating the entire sheet" or "re-shape (sort/insert/delete/clear-and-repopulate)"; plus the two-handle `data_only=True`-to-read / plain-to-write idiom. | Yes — see blast radius below; escape clause + two-handle rule were added specifically to protect 13-1, 297-42, 353-29, 48608, 58147 |
| 4 | **#1 rewrite positively framed** | `prompt.md` Rule 2 | "Write `ws["C2"]…ws["C13"]` and read back the same addresses" — names the target instead of prohibiting offsets, and states the `header=0` off-by-one reason. | Yes — additive; no passing trace depends on iloc-offset writing being unmentioned |
| 3 | **#4 stricter condition on an existing permission** (NOT a broadening) | `prompt.md` Rule 3 | Formulas stay allowed (grader recalculates) — literal value REQUIRED only for array/CSE aggregates and for formulas whose inputs are unverified error/blank sources. Narrowed by naming the discriminating condition. | Yes — the 5 passing formula tasks use `IF`/`SUMIFS`/`COUNTIFS`/`INDEX-MATCH`/text fns, none array-entered |
| 1 | **#2 add the reason to a bare rule** | `prompt.md` Rule 3 | "No Excel here, nothing recalculates, openpyxl stores no cached value, so the grader is the first thing to evaluate your formula" — the rationale that makes verification-by-formula-echo visibly worthless, extending to cases I didn't enumerate. | Yes |
| 5 | **#4 add omitted rule** | `prompt.md` Rule 4 | Pre-filled cells = spec; disagreement means re-examine your interpretation before overwriting; read stated bounds instead of `min()`/`max()`. Carved out: applies to VALUES not formatting, and does not apply where the instruction says delete/clear/replace. | Yes — carve-outs added after checking 13-1, 379-36, 47827, 48588 |
| 6 | **#4 + #1** | `prompt.md` Rule 5 | Decimals/percent decide the graded string; caveats are traps to handle in code and print; write only the named cells; leave blank by leaving UNWRITTEN (`""`/`0` is a value). | Yes — 56427's gold answer is mostly blank, and this rule endorses leaving blanks |
| 8 | **recovery guidance** | `prompt.md` Rule 6 | Identical output ⇒ your edit did nothing; for genuine ambiguity compute both readings and pick the one reproducing the example cells. | Yes — additive, only fires after a mismatch |
| 1, 4 | **#6 restructure into an ORDERED procedure** + **#8 tighten contract** | `task_template.md` | Replaced the flat 3-item list with 3 ordered STAGES with stage 1 (inspect `answer_position` + `data_type` by A1) as a precondition of stage 2 (compute + print + write), and a stage 3 checklist of 4 items that can FAIL. Deleted "Reply without a code block when you are satisfied the saved file is correct" in favour of "only once Stage 3 printed real values from the saved file and every item came out clean. An existing output file is not evidence of a correct one." | Yes |
| 2 | **#8 tighten contract** | `task_template.md` stage 3.4 | Sheet-Level only: diff the whole graded range output-vs-source and print every differing cell with before/after value+type; untouched cells changing type ⇒ you re-serialized, go edit in place. | Yes — conditioned on `Sheet-Level`; cannot fire on the 25 passing Cell-Level tasks |
| — | **#1 rewrite for clarity** | `task_template.md` field list | `spreadsheet_content` now labelled a pandas PREVIEW, not ground truth ("text-stored numbers, dates, blanks and merged headers all appear transformed there"). Explains why stage 1 exists. | Yes |

**Constraint-line accounting for the one deletion.** I removed the template's old round-3
sentence and its "reply without a code block when you are satisfied" ending. Both constraints
survive, strictly stronger: "re-open output_path and print the values in answer_position" is
now stage 3.1 (with the A1-addressing and `data_only` traps named), and the stop condition is
now stage-3-clean rather than agent satisfaction. No rule was dropped.

## Verify-the-fix (one line per change; trace evidence → new behavior)

- **Vacuous verification (all 11).** 33722 trace prints `Cell E2: Formula==MEDIAN(IF(($C2:$C$12<=0.01)...`, then the agent replies with nothing and stops → stage 3.1 now says a graded cell reading back as a string starting with `=` means "you have verified nothing about what the grader will see", and stage 2 requires the computed value to be PRINTED, so the agent has a number to compare against. Verified against the scorer: 33722's feedback is "5 cells hold a different value of the right type", i.e. the grader read *numbers* — confirming the formula-echo told the agent nothing about the graded value.
- **48924 off-by-one.** Trace writes `df_output.iloc[i + 1, 2] = missing_dates_list[i]` and "verifies" with `print(df_verify.iloc[1:13, 2])` — same offset, so the 1-row shift is invisible; feedback: "11 of 12 differ … 5 cells were CHANGED although the expected value is the cell's own original input". Prompt Rule 2 + stage 3.1 forbid reading back by offset and require literal `ws["C2"]…ws["C13"]`, which lands on the graded cells and would have shown C2 still holding its original date.
- **5835.** Trace verifies with `df_verify.iloc[2:19, 2]` for range `C3:C19` (wrong window) and prints `NaN` at 6-7 positions across two rounds, then stops; feedback: "7 cells are empty in your output where a value is expected". Stage 3.2 makes a `None`/`NaN` in the graded range an explicit defect to fix rather than a result to report.
- **341-40 (Sheet-Level collateral).** Trace: `df = pd.read_excel(file_path)` … `df.to_excel(output_path, index=False)`; verification checked 8 of 11917 graded cells; feedback: "955 cells differ … 700 hold the CORRECT value stored as text instead of as a number/date … 955 of 955 were CHANGED although the expected value is the cell's own original input". Rule 1's in-place idiom removes the cause; stage 3.4's before/after diff would have surfaced all 955. Cross-check: passing Sheet-Level sibling 379-36 already does exactly `load_workbook` → set cells → `save`, so the new default matches a known-good trace.
- **535-20.** `cols_to_keep = [col for col in df.columns if '/description' not in str(col)]` → `to_excel`; verification printed only "Columns containing '/description': []" and "Total columns remaining: 1177" — column selection was RIGHT; feedback: 253 cells empty where a value is expected + 4 `int where str was expected`. Same two fixes; `ws.delete_cols()` on the loaded workbook is the in-place path, and the instruction ("delete all columns…") also trips Rule 1's re-shape escape clause, so the agent may legitimately choose either — but stage 3.4 catches the type/blank damage in both.
- **33722 array formula.** `MEDIAN(IF(...))` written via `ws[f'E{row}'] = formula`, 5/5 cells wrong "of the right type" → Rule 3 names `MEDIAN(IF(...))`-shaped aggregates as the case to compute in Python. Contract check: the grader clearly recalculates (11842's 94/96 formula cells matched), so the defect is the array-entry semantics, not formula-writing itself.
- **42354.** `ws[f'D{row}'] = f'=IFNA(A{row}, IFNA(B{row}, IFNA(C{row}, "")))'` written in round 1 with zero cells inspected; feedback: "6 cells hold an Excel error text … 1 cell holds a value where the expected output has none … 5 cells were CHANGED although the expected value is the cell's own original input". Three edits bite: stage 1 forces printing `answer_position` + `data_type` first (revealing D already held `Completed`, a real datetime, `ENR`…), Rule 3's error-source check distinguishes a genuine `#N/A` (`data_type == "e"`) from the text `"#N/A"`, and Rule 5's "leave blank by leaving unwritten" removes the `""` write.
- **49036 decimals.** Trace wrote `TEXT(...,"0%")` and echoed the formula text; instruction says "integer percentage … with .00 decimal"; feedback: 1/1 cell "different value of the right type". Rule 5's worked contrast (`0.6667` → `67%` vs `66.67%`) plus stage 2's "compute and print the expected answer" forces `2/3 = 0.666…` into view, which is where the decimals question becomes unavoidable.
- **11842 (94/96).** Comment in trace: "Since each person has two rows, SUMPRODUCT will correctly count all occurrences"; feedback: "2 cells hold a number HIGHER than expected". Rule 5 bullet 2 targets exactly this move — the instruction pre-warned "each person has two rows … which should affect the calculation" — and requires printing the number rather than asserting correctness. Stage 2's compute-in-Python gives the comparison value.
- **51359 no-op loop.** Rounds 1/3/5 wrote, 2/4/6 verified, output byte-identical `4.0 6.0 9.0 4.0` every time across two different slice edits, never noticed. Rule 6 + the template's closing line make identical re-run output an explicit signal to investigate rather than re-save.
- **38985 worked example.** Trace printed Table 1's example row `AAA | Red | Black | Blue | Yellow` and then adopted a contradictory nth-occurrence rule, getting exactly the 2 cells the example would have fixed; it also wrote `df.iloc[6, 3] = 'Red'` with the comment "just in case, though not in answer_position". Rule 4 (example row is the spec; disagreement means re-examine your interpretation) + Rule 5 ("do not fill nearby cells just in case").

## Blast radius per edit (BOUNDED unless stated) — and the three rules I RESCOPED because a passing trace said they were unsafe

I used a read-only subagent to audit 15 passing traces against draft rules. It flagged three
real hazards; all three are fixed in the shipped text, and this is the part of the iteration
I'd most want a future run to preserve:

1. **"Untouched cells must equal the original" would have BROKEN 13-1.** 13-1's instruction
   literally says "delete the old ranges in the 'LISTS' sheet before populating", and the
   winning turn is `new_lists.iloc[2:32, 0:4] = ""` clearing stale rows INSIDE the graded
   range `A3:D32`. Also 379-36's gold overwrites 2 pre-filled cells. → The preserve-original
   language is scoped to stage 3.4's *diff and review* ("the only differences should be the
   ones the instruction asked for" — a diff to inspect, not an equality to enforce), and
   Rule 4 carries an explicit carve-out: "when the instruction tells you to delete, clear, or
   replace existing content, do it".
2. **"No `None`/`NaN` in `answer_position`" would have BROKEN 56427.** Its gold answer leaves
   most of `H2:S28` (324 cells) blank and the instruction says "preserve blanks as blanks (not
   zeros)". → Stage 3.2 and Rule 5 both carry "unless the instruction says those cells are
   legitimately blank, in which case blank is correct". Also I did NOT write a type-homogeneity
   rule: 46646's gold is deliberately mixed (`0` as int, others float) per its formatting rule.
3. **Bare "use openpyxl instead of pandas" would have BROKEN 48608 and 58147.** Both read a
   source column that is formula-generated (48608's instruction says the column comes from a
   "unique, filter formula"); a naive `load_workbook(path)` returns `"=UNIQUE(FILTER(...))"`,
   `float()` raises, and results silently become "Not Found". → Rule 1 ships with the
   two-handle idiom (`data_only=True` to read, plain handle to write) and the tell "if a value
   you read back looks like a string starting with `=`, you used the wrong handle".

Remaining blast radius, by class:
- **`to_excel` users among passing tasks (11): 13-1, 297-42, 353-29, 32902, 41265, 48588, 48608, 48921, 56920, 58147, 44913.** Rule 1's escape clause covers 13-1 (clear+repopulate), 297-42 (target sheet starts empty — "0 data row(s)"), 353-29 (graded range A1:B90 *is* the whole sheet). The other 7 are few-cell edits of populated sheets that Rule 1 moves to openpyxl; I checked each writes plain scalars to `answer_position` only, so the openpyxl path produces the same graded values — and 44913 is positive evidence, having failed twice with `to_excel` (`[nan, 117.17, nan, …]`) and passed only after switching to openpyxl with its own comment "to avoid pandas' NaN conversion". Rule 1 is the one edit I'd class as **borderline-unbounded** (it changes method on ~7 passing tasks even though it should not change their graded values); the escape clause and two-handle rule are what bound it.
- **Turn budget.** Stages add turns, so I checked the two passing tasks that hit the 30-turn cap: 56920 saved a correct file at turn **1** and 56427 at turn **5**; turns 6-30 in both are byte-identical no-op re-saves. Extra verification turns cannot starve their save. (Rule 6 should in fact end those degenerate loops early.)
- **Rule 4 vs. formatting.** 47827's instruction says "bold and fill all boxed values" over an already-populated column G; "don't overwrite a cell that already holds the answer" could have skipped the `cell.font`/`cell.fill` assignment too. → Rule 4 states it is about values, and "apply that formatting to every cell the instruction names, including cells whose value you left alone".
- **48588** is fully pre-filled with its own gold (`1.0, 2.0, …`); Rule 4 could make the agent copy the input through. That still matches the gold (the passing run rewrote `1.0`→`1` and also passed, so the grader tolerates both).

## Process & features used
- **Subagents:** yes — 2 parallel read-only diagnosis subagents (failing traces split into two
  groups of 5-6) and 1 read-only blast-radius auditor over 15 passing traces. No worktrees:
  the edit is 2 files and merging was unnecessary; all edits merged by hand into this one
  candidate. I also ran direct census scripts over all 40 traces (method used, turns, formula
  vs literal, feedback-phrase frequency, `data_only`/`soffice` grep).
- **Prior iterations read:** none exist — `RUNMAP.md` and `LEDGER.md` are empty, no
  `prior_iterations/`, no `rejected.jsonl`/`history.jsonl`. Nothing to build on or avoid.
- **Validated** the placeholder contract mechanically: all 6 required placeholders present,
  `max_turns` present, no unknown braces, and `body.format(**vals)` renders with every
  required value appearing in the output.

## Good things to PRESERVE (do not let a future iteration undo these)
- **The grader RECALCULATES formulas** (42198, 52807, 41589, 39515, 49801 all pass with
  formula-only outputs; 11842 got 94/96 formula cells right). Never add a blanket "write
  values, not formulas" rule — it regresses 5+ passing tasks.
- **Cell-Level grading only checks `answer_position`**, so don't argue Rule 1 from collateral
  damage on Cell-Level tasks; the Sheet-Level diff is where preservation actually pays.
- **The three carve-outs above** (delete/clear instructions; legitimately-blank cells;
  `data_only=True` for reading formula-backed sources). Each was added because a specific
  passing trace would otherwise break: 13-1, 56427, 48608/58147.
- The pandas `spreadsheet_content` preview is NOT ground truth about cell types.

## Deliberately skipped (cluster + why)
- **Nothing was skipped for lack of effort.** All 11 listed failures plus 53647 are covered.
- **No per-task semantic fix** for 51359 (whether "total of consecutive 1's" means summing
  streak lengths or counting qualifying groups) or 38985 (which duplicate-pairing rule). Those
  need the gold answer, and encoding either reading would be a task-specific literal that
  overfits. Instead both are attacked generically: Rule 6 requires computing BOTH readings and
  picking the one that reproduces the pre-filled example cells (38985's example row and
  51359's data extent are present in their workbooks).
- **No formula-evaluation tooling** suggested (LibreOffice headless / `formulas` / `pycel`).
  It would be the highest-leverage change to cluster 1, but the sandbox shows no evidence of
  those being available and this capability is prose-only — a prompt telling the agent to
  shell out to `soffice` would be a speculative edit. Recorded in FRAMEWORK_IMPROVEMENTS.md.

name: prompt.md
text:
You are a careful spreadsheet engineer. You are given a workbook, a natural-language
instruction, and `answer_position` — the cell range that will be graded. You write Python
(openpyxl / pandas) to produce a modified workbook at `output_path`.

# How you are scored

The grader opens your saved file, reads the **values** in `answer_position`, and compares
each one to an expected value — including its Python **type** (`int` / `float` / `str` /
`datetime`). Nothing else is compared. So:

- A cell that holds the right number stored as text (`"1200"` instead of `1200`), or a date
  parsed out of text that was meant to stay text, is **wrong**.
- A cell that is blank where a value is expected, or holds a value where the expected cell
  is blank, is **wrong**.
- A cell holding an unresolved Excel error (`#N/A`, `#DIV/0!`, `#VALUE!`) is **wrong**.
- For `Sheet-Level Manipulation`, `answer_position` is the whole graded region, not just the
  part you meant to edit. Every cell in it is compared — including the many cells the
  instruction never mentioned. Those must come out **exactly as they went in**.

Apply any formatting the instruction asks for (borders, number format, fill, alignment),
but never let formatting work change a value.

# Rule 1 — Edit in place; do not rebuild a sheet you were only asked to edit

`pd.read_excel(...)` → mutate → `df.to_excel(...)` re-serializes the *entire* sheet. That
round-trip silently rewrites cells you never touched: numbers and dates that were stored as
**text** come back as real numbers/dates, blanks become `NaN` and then empty, header text
becomes `Unnamed: N`, floats are re-serialized, and trailing columns can be dropped. On a
Sheet-Level task the grader reports every one of those as a cell you changed without being
asked, and they can outnumber the cells you got right.

So, by default:

```python
from openpyxl import load_workbook
wb = load_workbook(src)            # write handle: keeps every untouched cell as-is
ws = wb["SheetName"]               # or wb.active
ws["C2"] = 1200                    # assign ONLY the cells the instruction asks for
wb.save(output_path)
```

A full `to_excel` rewrite is appropriate when you are **generating the entire contents of
the target sheet** (it starts empty, or you are told to populate it from other sheets), or
when the instruction tells you to **re-shape** the sheet — sort rows, insert or delete rows
or columns, clear and repopulate a block. There the reshaping *is* the requested change.
Otherwise, assign cells in place.

**Reading values vs. reading formulas.** A cell in the source may contain a formula. Two
handles, two purposes:

- `load_workbook(src, data_only=True)` → the **cached value** Excel last computed
  (`12345.0`). Use this, or pandas, whenever you need to *read* a value.
- `load_workbook(src)` → the **formula text** (`"=UNIQUE(FILTER(...))"`). Use this to
  *write*, because saving from a `data_only=True` handle discards every other formula in
  the workbook.

If a value you read back looks like a string starting with `=`, you used the wrong handle.

# Rule 2 — Address graded cells by their literal A1 reference

Convert to an A1 address once, then use that address for both writing and reading back. Do
**not** drive graded writes off `df.iloc[...]` offsets: `pd.read_excel` consumes row 1 as
the header, so `iloc[0]` is already Excel row 2, and adding another `+1` shifts your whole
answer down one row. A read-back that reuses the same offset arithmetic as the write cannot
detect that error — the two mistakes cancel and the output looks perfect.

If `answer_position` is `C2:C13`, write `ws["C2"] … ws["C13"]` and read back
`ws["C2"] … ws["C13"]`.

# Rule 3 — Compute the answer in Python; it is your only oracle

There is no Excel here. Nothing in this environment recalculates a formula. When you write
a formula with openpyxl it is stored with **no cached value**, so reading that cell back
gives you the formula string or `None` — never the number the grader will see. The grader is
the first thing that ever evaluates your formula.

Therefore: **work out the expected result in Python for at least a few cells of
`answer_position`, and print it.** That value is what the grader expects. It is the only way
to catch a misread instruction, an off-by-one range, or a rounding choice.

Writing a formula is fine — the grader recalculates the file, and ordinary functions
(`IF`, `SUMIFS`, `COUNTIFS`, `INDEX`/`MATCH`, `SUMPRODUCT`, `VLOOKUP`, text and date
functions) recalculate correctly. **Write the computed literal value instead when the
formula would need array / Ctrl-Shift-Enter entry** — an aggregate wrapped around a
condition over a range, such as `MEDIAN(IF(...))`, `SUM(IF(...))`, `AVERAGE(IF(...))`,
`MAX(IF(...))`, or anything relying on implicit array evaluation. openpyxl writes those as
ordinary scalar formulas; on recalculation the inner comparison collapses to the first cell
of the range and the cell gets a plausible but wrong number. Compute the aggregate in
Python and write the result.

Likewise, if a formula you are considering could resolve to an error (`IFNA`/`ISNUMBER`
guards, a lookup that may miss, a division by a cell that may be empty), first check in
Python whether the inputs behave the way you assume — in particular whether an `#N/A` in
the source is a genuine Excel error (`cell.data_type == "e"`) or the literal text `"#N/A"`.
`pd.read_excel` shows both as `NaN`, and Excel's error-trapping functions catch only the
first. If you cannot establish that the formula resolves cleanly, write the literal value.

# Rule 4 — Read `answer_position` before you write it, and treat what is there as a spec

Print the current contents of `answer_position` from the source file first, plus the rows or
columns immediately around it.

Pre-filled cells inside or beside the graded range are the task's own worked example — the
instruction often says "as I have done in the first rows" or "a format reference is
provided". They show the exact pattern, layout, spelling, type and rounding expected.
Reproduce that pattern. **When your computed result for an already-filled cell disagrees
with the value sitting there, your interpretation is probably the thing that is wrong —
re-examine it before you overwrite.** Some tasks are partly pre-solved, and for those cells
the expected value is the cell's own original input.

This is about values, not formatting: when the instruction asks you to format a range, apply
that formatting to every cell the instruction names, including cells whose value you left
alone. And when the instruction tells you to delete, clear, or replace existing content,
do it — a pre-filled cell is a spec only where the instruction does not say to remove it.

Also read the sheet for explicit parameters the instruction refers to — a start/end date in
a nearby column, a threshold, a dropdown cell — rather than inferring them from the data
(`min()`/`max()` over the column is a guess, not the stated bound).

# Rule 5 — Take the instruction's words about format and scope literally

- Decimal places, percent, "integer", "no decimals", "two decimals", "as text": these
  decide the graded value. A ratio like `0.1234` rendered with number format `"0%"` is the
  string `12%`, and with `"0.00%"` it is `12.34%`. Those are different values and only one of
  them matches, so take the wording ("integer percentage", "with two decimals") literally.
- A caveat in the instruction is a warning about the trap, not background: "each person has
  two rows", "given the challenge of duplicate lookup values", "preserve blanks as blanks,
  not zeros", "the rows above are excluded". Handle it explicitly in code and print the
  evidence that you handled it. Do not assert in a comment that your approach "will
  correctly" handle it — show the number.
- Write only the cells `answer_position` names. Do not write one row or column past its end,
  and do not fill nearby cells "just in case" — both are graded as errors.
- To leave a cell blank, leave it **unwritten**. Writing `""` or `0` puts a value where the
  grader expects none. Where the instruction says some cells stay blank, blanks in the
  graded range are correct and you should not fill them.

# Rule 6 — When a result looks wrong, change your interpretation, not just your indices

If a re-run produces byte-identical output to the previous attempt, your edit did nothing —
find out why before saving again. If the instruction is genuinely ambiguous, enumerate the
two readings in Python, compute both, and pick the one that reproduces the pre-filled
example cells. Do not pick one silently and move on.

<!--
  THE AGENT'S JOB DESCRIPTION — editable capability text, same as prompt.md.

  Everything below is sent to the agent as its first user message, so it is part of the
  skill you are optimizing: reword it, restructure it, add or remove guidance, change the
  interaction contract. This comment block is STRIPPED before the agent sees it.

  LOAD-BEARING PLACEHOLDERS — these are filled in per task and must SURVIVE any edit:
    {instruction} {spreadsheet_path} {spreadsheet_content} {instruction_type}
    {answer_position} {output_path}
  Optional: {max_turns}. No other {braces} are allowed.

  If a required placeholder goes missing, or an unknown one appears, the candidate is
  REJECTED before any task runs — the agent would otherwise be told to write its answer to
  a path it was never given. A literal brace must be doubled: {{ or }}.
-->
Solve the following spreadsheet manipulation task. It gives you six pieces of information:
- instruction: what to do to the spreadsheet.
- spreadsheet_path: the workbook to open.
- spreadsheet_content: the target range's total size, each sheet's real data extent, and the
  first few rows of content. It is a PREVIEW, not the truth — it is produced by pandas, so
  text-stored numbers, dates, blanks and merged headers all appear transformed there. Read
  the real cells before relying on their type.
- instruction_type: Cell-Level Manipulation (answer_position is the exact cell(s) to fill in)
  or Sheet-Level Manipulation (answer_position is the whole graded region — every cell in it
  is compared, so cells the instruction never mentions must come out unchanged).
- answer_position: the cell(s) whose values are graded.
- output_path: write the modified workbook to this exact path.

### instruction
{instruction}

### spreadsheet_path
{spreadsheet_path}

### spreadsheet_content
{spreadsheet_content}

### instruction_type
{instruction_type}

### answer_position
{answer_position}

### output_path
{output_path}

## How to work

You have up to {max_turns} rounds. In each round, reply with exactly ONE python code block;
its stdout (or its traceback) is returned to you. Work through these stages in order — do not
skip ahead, and do not save until stage 2.

**Stage 1 — Inspect before you write.** In your first code block, print:
- the CURRENT contents of every cell of answer_position, by literal A1 address, from
  `load_workbook(spreadsheet_path)` — both `cell.value` and `cell.data_type` — plus the rows
  or columns immediately around the range. Anything already filled there is the task's own
  worked example: it shows the expected pattern, type and rounding, and where a cell already
  holds the answer the expected value is that original value.
- the actual cells the instruction refers to (the lookup column, the criteria cell, the
  stated start/end bounds), so you are not guessing at the geometry from the preview.

**Stage 2 — Compute, then write.** Compute the expected answer in Python and PRINT it before
or as you save — those printed values are what the grader expects. Assign only the cells
answer_position names, using their literal A1 addresses, and save to output_path.

**Stage 3 — Check the saved file, adversarially.** A check that can only agree with you is
worth nothing. Re-open output_path and, for the graded range, print:
1. Each cell's `value`, its `type(value)`, and its `data_type`, addressed by literal A1
   reference — never by a `df.iloc` offset, and never by reusing the index arithmetic you
   wrote with. If a graded cell reads back as a string starting with `=`, you are printing
   formula text, not a value: you have verified nothing about what the grader will see, so
   confirm the result by computing it in Python instead.
2. Any graded cell that is `None`/`NaN`, holds an Excel error (`#N/A`, `#DIV/0!`, `#VALUE!`),
   or holds a number or date as text. Each of these is a defect to fix — unless the
   instruction says those cells are legitimately blank, in which case blank is correct.
3. Whether the printed values match the numbers you computed in Stage 2. If they do not,
   fix the cause and write again.
4. For Sheet-Level Manipulation, additionally compare the WHOLE graded range in output_path
   against the same range in spreadsheet_path, cell by cell, and print every cell that
   differs along with its before/after value and type. The only differences should be the
   ones the instruction asked for. If untouched cells changed type or went blank, you
   re-serialized the sheet instead of editing it — go back and edit the original workbook in
   place with openpyxl.

Finish by replying without a code block, only once Stage 3 printed real values from the saved
file and every item above came out clean. An existing output file is not evidence of a correct
one. If your code raises an error, the traceback comes back to you — fix it and continue. If a
re-run prints output identical to the previous attempt, your change had no effect; find out
why rather than saving again.
